cues.text: A Widow at Twenty-Eight
Born on January 28, 1572, at Dijon, France, the daughter of the president of the Parliament of Burgundy, Jane Frances Frémyot was married in 1592 to the Baron de Chantal.

By every surviving account, their nine years together were a genuinely happy marriage; Jane brought considerable practical skill to running the family's declining estate, restoring both its finances and its household order.
Her happiness ended abruptly in 1601, when Christophe was killed in a hunting accident.
Jane became a widow of twenty-eight with four young children and a difficult, embittered father-in-law.
Under his roof, she was obliged to live for the next seven years.
A Vow Amid Trial
Jane bore her father-in-law's harsh treatment with a patience that cost her real suffering, and during these same difficult years took a private vow of perpetual chastity, resolving never to remarry.
Throughout this trial she prayed constantly for God to send her a spiritual guide equal to the weight of what she was carrying.
She reported having received, in prayer, an inward vision of the very director providence held in reserve for her — though she did not yet know his face or name.
Recognizing Francis de Sales
In Lent of 1604, visiting her own father at Dijon, Jane heard Francis de Sales , then Bishop of Geneva, preach a series of sermons.
By her own account, she recognized in him the very director she had seen in her earlier vision.
Francis became her spiritual guide for the rest of his life.
Their correspondence—patient, direct, and full of genuine spiritual friendship—fills volumes.
Jane herself destroyed most after his death, out of a reverence she judged too personal to leave behind for others to read.
Founding the Visitation
Once her children's futures were properly secured, Jane traveled to Annecy in 1610 to help Francis found a new kind of religious community.
It was intended for women whose age, health, or family circumstances excluded them from the severe physical austerities most existing orders required.

The Congregation of the Visitation of Holy Mary was established there on Trinity Sunday, June 6, 1610, envisioned at first as an unenclosed community whose sisters would go out to nurse the sick and serve the poor directly.
A Refuge for the Rejected
Ecclesiastical opposition to women religious moving freely outside the cloister eventually obliged Francis to make the Visitation fully enclosed under the Rule of St. Augustine.
For this order, he composed his celebrated Treatise on the Love of God, but Jane never abandoned its original spirit of welcome.

She accepted candidates other orders had turned away for poor health or advanced age, once receiving a woman of eighty-three, and answered critics simply: she liked sick people herself, and was on their side.
Sustained Loss, Sustained Governance
Jane governed the growing Visitation through a succession of severe personal losses: Francis de Sales's death in 1622, her own son's death in battle, and a plague that ravaged France.
Against the plague, she opened her convents' resources without reserve, while also enduring the deaths of both a daughter-in-law and a son-in-law.

Alongside these griefs, she bore long interior seasons of spiritual dryness and darkness, by every account, without ever relaxing her governance of the order or care for the many who sought her counsel.
Legacy

Jane died at the Visitation convent in Moulins on December 13, 1641, at sixty-nine, while making an official visitation of the order's convents; by then the community numbered eighty-six houses, grown from the original three.
She was beatified in 1751 and canonized in 1767; her body rests today beside that of Francis de Sales in the church of the Visitation at Annecy.
Honored across her whole life as daughter, wife, mother, widow, and foundress, Jane Frances de Chantal remains a rare and complete witness.
Sanctity asks nothing of a single state in life, but only the same total, patient fidelity, carried faithfully through whatever state God happens to place before us.
